Harold Mabern
Pianist Harold Mabern was born in Memphis, Tennessee on March 20, 1936.

He has shared the stage and studio with J.J. Johnson, Frank Strozier, Joe Williams and numerous others. Harold has enjoyed a long tenure as an instructor at William Paterson University and he records frequently with saxophonist Eric Alexander, one of his notable students.
Harold was interviewed at Hamilton College on March 31, 2010 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and I am very pleased to have pianist Harold Mabern with me today for the Jazz Archive. Welcome to Hamilton.
Thank you.
It’s been a real pleasure listening to your numerous stories the last couple of days.
Oh boy.
You are not a shy man.
Well you know I try not to be.
I’m wondering if you were an outgoing kid?

You know strangely enough I was very shy. Believe it or not I was very quiet, very shy. But as I got a little older I got a little more, how do you put it, outgoing and aggressive in my manner so to speak, when I moved to Chicago. But during the time I was in Memphis, Tennessee I was really a quiet, shy kid you know.
I’m wondering, you know, we think of Memphis as a heavy blues town.
Right.
Did you hear blues a lot growing up in the home?

We heard it in the home, and when I started getting into music, which was around the age of 15 or 16, see I’m a late bloomer, you know because being a self-taught musician I never took piano lessons. We had to play the blues because that was the way it was. And we were drugged and we were disappointed because we wanted to play bebop. And the club owners would say no, no, you’ve got to get that bebop out of here, you’re running my customers out of here, in other words we had to play music that they could dance to. So what we did and when I say we I’m speaking of a lot about George Coleman’s brother, who was a very good alto saxophonist. I played along with George Coleman’s brother before I played with George Coleman. George Coleman’s brother, Lucius Coleman, Louis Smith, a drummer named Big Moe, and that was it because we didn’t have but two or three bass players, and Jamil Nasser was one. He was out with B.B. King. So most times the piano players had to walk the bass line. So what we would do, © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

we would play the blues, say “The Hucklebuck,” which you later found out was “Now’s The Time,” but it’s really “The Hucklebuck,” Paul Williams “Hucklebuck” [scats]. So we would tell the drummer, you know, keep the backbeat while the people would dance. And then, once we got them dancing, we started playing the chord changes to “All the Things You Are,” or “Perdido.” That’s how we got over. And the club owner would walk over and say, “That’s much better, that’s what I’m talking about.” He never knew the difference, as long as the drummer, you know, kept the backbeat going. But like I say we were drugged because we says man we got to play these blues, but now, some 30, 40, 50 years later we realize what a blessing in disguise it was because everybody can’t play the blues. Charles Mingus said, “I want to write like Duke Ellington and play the blues.” The great Dizzy Gillespie, the coprogenetist of this music said “the difference between me and Bird is that Bird can play the blues and I couldn’t. And that’s what Dizzy said on videotape, which we knew that. I mean everybody can’t play — it’s something that you can’t teach. That’s the phenomenal thing about Eric Alexander as he was saying earlier. There are benefits of all jobs. He learned how to play the blues by being with Charles Earland, an association. And that’s how that came about. We never talked about that, like Eric I’m going to teach you how to play the blues, because I can’t because if I could teach somebody how to play the blues I would have gone to Gene Harris and said hey Gene, see because he could play the blues you see.
Well let me ask you about this Memphis, the clubs. How old were you when you started doing that?
About 15-1/2 or 16 years old.
Okay. How did your parents feel about you playing in these dance clubs?

Well they didn’t have a problem with it, I guess they were just happy to see me try and pursue something rather than being in the streets, even though the streets, being in the streets then was nothing like it is now as far as what the young kids are doing. The things they do now we didn’t even think about doing stuff like that. So they were always supportive of me because, like I say, they loved the blues, and we went to church, I had to go to church all the time, two or three times on a Sunday you know. But they always, you know, supported me. Because even though my mother was around, she and my father had separated for a while so I was raised up with my father, my aunt and my grandmother. But I still had a chance to be with my mother during that time.
But you had this interest in bebop, and where did that come from at that age? Was it by the radio or buying LPs?

No, see that’s the thing. On the radio you didn’t hear no — first of all, on the radio you would hear maybe some Dave Brubeck and some George Shearing, but you didn’t really hear no Art Tatum, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, at that time because that was too strong © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

for the airways. So even then, the artists who played that way had to play in a more commercial-type vein. But we always had big bands that would come to Memphis, like the Count Basie big band, or the Duke Ellington big band, or the Lionel Hampton Orchestra and they would play it at the Palace Theater and on that group would be like a big band, a jazz vocalist, maybe Sarah Vaughan or Ella Fitzgerald or something like that, and a comedian, and that would be it. So we had a chance to hear it that way. Otherwise we would just, some of the guys were hip enough to have had the records by Bud Powell and Charlie Parker and we used to go by their houses and listen. That’s how we got exposed to it. But strange enough George Coleman and Louis Smith and Phineas Newborn, they already were hip to Charlie Parker, the hard edge, hard core, bebop if you will.
I see. Were the clubs segregated at that time?
Yes. The clubs were segregated at the time but there were a couple of artists [who] would be able to come in, but for the most part all the clubs were segregated, yeah.
And this would have been around 19 —
1950, ’51, ’52 and on up, yeah.
So your repertoire of blues would include tunes like “The Hucklebuck.”
“The Hucklebuck,”
“Night Train.”
“Night Train,” “The Boogie Woogie,” a lot of slow blues with the singing, with the vocalist singing and stuff like that.
What were the pianos like that you got to play on?

Very bad. I mean really bad. See you know I think that probably most of the great piano players that would want to came up. Art Tatum played on bad pianos. Phineas Newborn Jr. had two pianos, both of them were bad. So there were no Steinways during that time. As a matter of fact they were all uprights. Very bad, keys missing, ivories jagged so if you’re not careful you’d cut your finger. Oh that was some bad times. But we had to deal with what we had. And a lot of times the pianos would be so out of tune, that’s how I think I learned how to transpose. I’d have to do crossover and I’d have to play in one key while they played in another key to match the sound.
I’ll be darned.
So I think that’s how I began to learn how to transpose. Because I had to do it back then.
Well, almost like a guitar had a capo on it or something.
Right. What they call a bar. You slide that bar down there, yeah, that kind of thing, yeah.
That’s interesting. So was there any mixing between the white and the black musicians at this time? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Very, very little. Yes. I really can’t call it integrated, no, ‘cause like I said because it was before the total segregation. But what we would do, we could go to places like West Memphis, Arkansas, which was like across the bridge from us, and we would play in the white-owned club for the white audience, but it was totally segregated.
Interesting. Well you said something about going to Chicago because you thought you were going to get into —

Right. See when I graduated, [s/l] Frank Rhodes and I graduated from high school in 1954, so my sister and my brother-in-law and my mother were living in Chicago at the time. So she said well you come here and we’ll try to send you to the Chicago Conservatory of Music. Because I had about three or four scholarships, one to Tennessee State, Arkansas State, Jackson College and some other place. But I turned them down because I wanted to be able to get to Chicago which was a larger city and a better environment musically speaking. But when I got there the money situation was not what it could have been so my sister said well look, we can’t afford the college but since you’re here just stay here and see what you can do, which is what I did. I stayed there and hung out in the streets of Chicago and went to all the clubs, made the rounds and made all the jam sessions and I just said the rest is history you know.
Did you have music scholarships to these places?

Yeah I had music scholarships. Because see I played in the high school band. I played baritone horn in the high school band. I played the marches, “Colonel Bogie” marches, “Washington Post” and all that stuff. So I had a scholarship based on that. And at that time I was playing very little piano because I couldn’t, but most of it was because of my so-called expertise in the marching band.
Okay, but your piano playing was and is mostly self-taught.

All self-taught. All self-taught. As a matter of fact I went to the Chicago Conservatory and I went down, and I took a couple of lessons, but what it was was a case where I was memorizing the music. You probably heard this before from different people. It was like I was memorizing the music quicker than I could — like I’d look at it and say “The Happy Farmer” [scats] so I’d kind of like look at it and kind of pick it out. But then the next lesson it was like I had it memorized. I’d heard it by other people. But as far as formal training, no, I never really had any.
So when you were presented with the, let’s say someone that you were listening to was playing some kind of chord and you’d go oh man, what is that.
Right.
How do you go about finding out what that is?
Well before I left, the band director, George Coleman, George Coleman knows a lot about chords, they would show me. I knew after I started playing I began to understand, © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

oh well this is a G minor to C seven, like that. So I was kind of getting a little handle on it there. And then I could read, we had a little fake book called “The Warren’s Black Chord Book,” it was about that wide and that high, and all it had in there if it would have “Body and Soul” it would have E flat. Now you had to figure out E flat minor, E flat major, E flat what. But no melody notes or nothing. So we’d use that for certain tunes. But then once I got to Chicago, that’s when my ear training kind of opened and I really started to get down with chords and everything. So I never did really have a problem reading the chord changes once I saw what it was, but formal training, I didn’t have any of that. But the environment in Chicago was so healthy and so vast because here in Memphis you’d have maybe one or two great piano players. But in Chicago you might have five or six on every corner that could play. Because the city was a larger city, naturally.
Did you do any of the blues gigs on the south side or was that not something you pursued?

No. Well strange enough, I worked a lot in a big band on the south side with the Morris Ellis Big Band. He was the wonderful trombonist that went to school at Howard University with Benny Golson and Eddie Jones. He used to play up in Count Basie’s band. And so that’s how I got my little bit of big band training, by playing in a big band. And the charts were kind of, you know for somebody self-taught, they weren’t really too easy, but I was able to hang in there and get the experience that I needed. And after that when I moved to New York I was able to get right in Lionel Hampton’s band. So the experience I had in Chicago was good for me to play the music in Hamp’s band because I’d been reading music, you know, in the big band in Chicago.
Yeah. What was the pay scale back in Chicago in those days. What kind of money would you make on a gig?

Well if you made, say if you made 45 dollars on a weekend, that was a lot of money. If you made a gig, like a private party where you made 75 or a 100 dollars, oh man, that was fantastic. But I would say the basic pay would be something like 45 dollars per night. And what I would do is I would get that 45 dollars and go straight to Citibank, if I must say, not that I’m pushing them, and put it in, and I saved up. So when it was time for me to make my move to New York City I had the money already saved up.
Oh. That’s thinking ahead. But New York was like, okay, we have to go there.

Yeah, you’ve got to go because you go to play, say in Chicago, you’ve got to know when to make your move. After you say well we’ve done everything we can do here, it’s time to make the move to the Big Apple. Now see New York City, you never make the move because you’re never not there because there’s things to be done, even now, I mean just the city itself. But no matter what town you’re in, you can be in L.A. or Memphis or Chattanooga, whatever. There comes a time when you say, well we’ve gone as far as we © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

can go because we had a good group in Chicago called the MJT + 3, young people. Frank Strozier, Bob Cranshaw, Walter Perkins, myself, Bobby Bryant, you know. And we were very successful during that time. There were three groups that had hit records: Ahmad Jamal Trio, Ramsey Lewis Trio, and our group, you know. But after the work kind of subsided we said okay, it’s time to make the move to New York, which is what we did, because when we went to New York we had work lined up. We didn’t go there just to be checking it. We already had at least six to eight weeks’ work lined up, in and around the New York area.
You’re talking about—
MJT + 3.
Okay. Did that require that you have some kind of agent or something?
Well we had some kind of little agent. Sarah Vaughan, one of Sarah Vaughan’s husbands, he was kind of managing us. He was more of a manager than an agent I guess it’s one entity, you know.
Well what was New York like for you the first time that you got there?

Oh, overwhelming. I couldn’t believe it. Even though I had read about it and seen pictures, but I couldn’t believe what I could hear, really, for all intents and purposes by myself, but even George Coleman was there and Booker Little because at that time, they were working with Max Roach’s group. But as far as family members, I was on my own. And I said at that point, you know, I was mature enough to know how to handle it and everything. I knew how to manage whatever little money I had, and not go through it. And the thing was, we wanted to be in New York at least six months, which was the requirement, that you had to be there to get your union card. So before you could get your union card you’d be considered like a traveling musician, even though you’re in New York. And when the union man comes out you’d have to have like a thing to say, well I’m a traveling musician and I’m trying to establish residency here so I can eventually get my union card, which is what I finally did.
And you could still play?
You could still play.
Until you got the card.
Until you got the card.
Yeah. The union was pretty strong back then wasn’t it?

Oh yeah. They would come around and check your union card. It’s not quite like that now but during that time, oh, they would come around, “Okay young man let me see your union card.” Now if you come and tell them I don’t have one or something, what do you mean you don’t — you know what I mean? Oh yeah, they were very — I don’t think they do that as much now as they used to. And then they’d say we want you at the union hall © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Monday morning at eight o’clock, and you’d have to come and explain why you didn’t have a union card.
Wow. And when you finally were able to get in, did you have to do any auditioning for them?

Not really. The only requirement was that okay, you want to join the union, you’ve been here six months or whatever it is, now you’ve got to have the amount of money it takes to join the union, which was, maybe during that time, I don’t know it might have been 50 or 75 or 100 dollars, which was a lot of money during that time. Now I’m sure it’s much, much more and the requirements are stronger. I don’t think you have to do an audition but there are certain things that are stronger.
So you start to get established, and what was the Lionel Hampton gig like for you?

Very interesting. What happened, I got to New York and as I was telling a couple of students today, they wanted to know how did I motivate myself and get ahead. I said go to all the jam sessions. Even if it’s not a jam session, if you go to hear somebody play and you feel you’re sure you can play, try to do that. So Lionel Hampton was working at a place called the Metropole Lounge, on Seventh Avenue around 47, 48th street. And he wasn’t using a piano player. You know he was using guitar. Bill Maker was playing guitar
Who was that?

So one of my dearest friends from Chicago named John Neeley, rest his soul, he said why don’t you come by and sit in with Gates we called him. Lionel Hampton called him, “Hey Gates, come on Gates.” You know. So I went by and he introduced me to — and the Metropole was like a long bar, it was long and the band was spread out. You know it wasn’t too wide, just long. So John Neeley introduced me and said, “Hey this is Harold Mabern, he’s from Chicago, can he sit in?” And he said, “Yeah, Gates, you want to play something?” So I got up there, and naturally I knew “Flying Home” from the get go. And because I had been reading music in the big band in Chicago, my eyes were kind of up. And Hamp’s music wasn’t that extreme, it was mostly chords, not a lot of notes, maybe a little passage here. So I sat in and he said, “Yeah, Gates, yeah Gates, I like you” he said, “yeah, Gates, you want to go to Argentina with me?” I said yeah, you know, I didn’t even know if I had a passport then. So he said, “Okay Gates, you’ve got to come down here Thursday and the doctor will be here to give you vaccinations, you know, and you go down and get your passport. During that time you could go to the passport office at Rockefeller Center, you know, like 49th and what was it, Fifth Avenue. So I got my passport. Now one of Hamp’s agents, he was booked by Joe Glaser. And the tickets were already bought for the plane flight. So I think, some kind of way, I took somebody else’s seat. I don’t know who, you know. He said, “Yeah Gates.” So I got there, got my © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

vaccinations on that Thursday, that Friday I was on my way to Buenos Aires Argentina, and that’s how that happened. So I stayed with the band for a whole year, because, like I said, but at some point I was getting a little tired because I wanted to really play, that’s why I was in New York. I said a big band was one thing but I’m not getting that many solos. Then when I would get a solo, Hamp would come and start playing two fingers at the top so I was really getting a little tired of that. So we did about a six week tour, all through Europe, everywhere. All one nighters, oh man, all one nighters. You know. And what we when we would do a gig, even over there, we would find a place to go jam. They called them hot clubs. And we played tunes like “Straight Street,” John Coltrane’s “Straight Street” and stuff like that. And we would tell Hamp and he’d say, “Hey Gates, you all hanging out tonight?” And we’d say, “Oh no, we’re not hanging out tonight because we’d have Hamp hanging around.” He would get up there and want to play the same songs he’d been playing and come back and do the two piano thing. So when we got back to the States I was living in the Sloan House Y, which was good because I was only paying zero point 75 cents a day. Could you imagine that?
Say that again?
Zero point 75 cents a day.
What was the name of the place?

The Sloan House YMCA. 34th Street between Eighth and Ninth Avenue. Because I had five thousand dollars when I got there. In 1959 five thousand dollars was probably like what, 20 or 30 thousand dollars, because the cost of living was down. I mean Transcontinental Airlines from New York to Chicago by [Inaudible] was 24 dollars and 50 cents. The Four Seasons, the Sheraton, the Waldorf was like 50 dollars a week. You go there now, the occupancy rate is 65 dollars a night. That’s aside from the 300 or 499 dollars, you know. So five thousand dollars was a lot of money. Five thousand dollars is a lot of money now. If somebody just said I’m going to give you five thousand dollars for a piano lesson or a half hour gig, you know. So but I said I’m going to hold on to this money. How can I stretch it? Because we were staying at a hotel in midtown Manhattan called the Flanders. A lot of musicians stayed there. And I think that was something like 10 or 15 dollars a week. But I said I’ve got to make this money — because once this money goes if I don’t preserve it and get some gigs I’m going to be back in Chicago and I had no intention of doing that. So somebody told me about the Y. And I went there and I said okay, I can handle this. Private rooms you know. But you had to go to go to the main bathroom to take a shower. They had a lot of face bowls and stuff, it was big and roomy but you had to pick your time to get your showers in, for your privacy. So then I said but at this point I saved my money and I said I’m going to get an apartment. So I was able to get an apartment on 130 West 73rd Street, like a one-room kitchenette, it was 96 dollars a © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

month, which wasn’t bad. Now I’m sure that same place — I go by there sometimes and look at the building — I’m sure that place probably rents for five thousand dollars a month. The same place. So I said I need a phone, so I called the phone company. First thing, “Do you have any references?” I said, “Yeah I play with Lionel Hampton’s Orchestra. They checked it out, telephone, no problem. So the gig worked that way. So now we’re getting ready to go to Wildwood, New Jersey. So Cedar Walton, one of my dearest friends, called and said, “Brother Mabern, we’re down here at Birdland with the Jazztet, you know, Art Farmer, Benny Golson, Cedar Walton, Tootie Heath and probably Tommy Williams on bass. And he says, “You might want to come and sit in” you know. And I took him on. Because I was only one stop from Birdland on the subway, you know, where I lived. So I went down and Cedar introduced me to Benny Golson. But Benny Golson and Art, they kind of knew me from Chicago anyway with the MJT + 3. So I sat in and I don’t know what we played, something kind of like here, it might have been a blues, but I started playing. See I’ve always loved to comp. That’s my passion. You know I tell people I’m more concerned about being a great comper than a great soloist, because if I comp good then I feel I have a chance to get more jobs. So I started comping and I look up and I see Benny Golson smiling you know. And Art Farmer never did show much emotion. He had his horn out here and Tommy McIntosh, yeah, he was smiling. So when he got through playing and Benny Golson said, “Yeah Mabern, man, yeah, wow.” Whatever. And Art Farmer said, “Hey man, Benny and I we really didn’t” — you know because they were very unhappy because Cedar Walton was getting ready to leave to go with Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. Cedar Walton, Reggie Workman, Freddie Hubbard and Curtis Fuller went with that group. See that’s the thing in New York even then. Gigs were turning over. And if you happened to be in the right place you could get a gig if you could halfway play. The cat would say, “You want to sit in?” And if you could halfway play and swing, and I was always a good comper, a pretty good comper, and whatever little solo I played it swung, because I listened a lot to Wynton Kelly, one of my heroes you know. So I sat in so Art Farmer said, “Hey man, we’re getting ready to make a change and we got somebody kind of but if we hear anything we’ll let you know.” I said, “Okay, I’m going on back home to my apartment, because I’m going to Wildwood, New Jersey the next morning.” So around eight o’clock in the morning the telephone rings. I said, “Hello?” He said, “Yes, this is Art Farmer.” I said, “Yes.” I thought why is he calling me? He said, “Benny and I talked it over and we want you to join the band.” Just on the way I was comping. I’m not bragging but that’s all it was, the way I was comping and supporting them. So I said, “Well how do you want me to play?” And so Art says, “Just the way you did last night.” So at this time Benny Golson writes hard music. There are certain people that write music that write hard with a purpose: Thad © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Jones, Frank Foster, Benny Golson, Slide Hampton. You know, certain ones, if I’ve got to play some of that music, get it to me ten weeks ahead of time, you know. So I told Art, I said, “Well you know Art, you know you’re playing all those hard piano parts.” So Benny said, “Don’t worry, Mabern, we’re kind of getting away from that.” Because this time, this would have been the third Jazztet from the original with McCoy Tyner. Then Cedar. Now I’m coming it and that’s the third Jazztet. So sure enough they cut back on some but I still had certain kinds of music to read. So then I got in the band so Lionel Hampton says, “Gates, I’m going to take you to court, I’m going to sue you, I told you to stay with me, I was going to make you big as bubble gum.” That was his saying, you know. But we kind of worked it out, you know, because by rights you’re supposed to give two weeks notice and I think I gave five days notice or something. Because I said at this point I can not miss this gig. I mean this is a chance to really get out in the forefront. A band from New York, be on the scene, you know what I mean? Too good to be true, you know. So but we worked it out and he wished me well because at one point in time Benny Golson and Art Farmer had both been in his band, aside from Art Blakey, Lionel Hampton had more all-stars in his band than anybody had ever had: Clifford Brown, Gigi Gryce or Quincy Jones playing trumpet, Art Farmer, Alan Dawson or Johnny Griffin.
Dexter Gordon.
You name it. You know what I mean?
Even Joe Wilder played with him.
Everybody went through there. George Coleman was in there for a minute.
Well wasn’t that band, maybe not at the time, but considered to be sort of like a stopping point.
Yeah.
I’ll be here for a while —
For a while, right.
Because he didn’t pay great, did he?

He didn’t pay good. Well but let’s face it though, but he paid what was the going rate during that time, because I know they’d give you money in this envelope and they’d have all the deductions. It was 165 a week. But after the 165 I was able to save a hundred dollars. You see what I’m saying? So that still was a lot of money. If I could save a hundred dollars a week, hey man, you kidding? So I’d take that 65 and stretch it and pay my little phone bill, maybe my phone bill might have been what ten or fifteen dollars a month? You know what I’m saying? So that was the going — it was 165.
And were you still single at the time?

I’m still single at the time, yeah. So then when I got with the Jazztet, that was, as a matter of fact there’s a book out now that was put out by the Baroness Rothschild called © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Musicians’ Three Wishes. And she would go around with a camera and ask the musicians if they had three wishes what would that be. And come to find out I’m in the book. I never had no idea. I don’t even recall her or anybody talking to me. Because see here again, I would go to hear Thelonious Monk I would sit at the table with the band but I was well reserved and I knew how to keep my mouth shut and not speak until I was spoken to. And see even then, the older musicians liked me because I wasn’t one to run my mouth, like I knew, I would listen, and when they spoke to me. So I said, “Are you kidding?” and Michael West said, “Yeah Mabern, you’re in that book.” There’s two beautiful pictures, one with me and Charlie Rouse and one with me and Teddy Wilson, another one of my heroes, you know. Shortly after that we went to the Lionel jazz festival and we left there and probably went to Chicago and that’s where I met my wife, when I was with the Jazztet. And I used to say Benny Golson — then I thought about it and I said, now Benny Golson’s on the spot. He’s responsible for hiring me, but it was Cedar Walton that made it possible for me to sit in. So I said, “Cedar I’ve been with my wife almost fifty years, maybe because of you.” He said, “Brother Mabern, I didn’t know that.” So that’s how, and then I stayed with the band until it disbanded. I was with the band, we did two records together with the band and I did one beautiful quartet date with Art Farmer called “Perception” with Roy McCurdy, Tommy Williams and myself. A beautiful date. And like I always told Sonny [inaudible], he likes it, I said well, on any kind of job don’t leave the job unless the job leaves you. That’s my philosophy. As long as the job is going, don’t leave the job. Why should I go looking for something that already — you know what I mean? So I never quit a job, I stayed until it was over then I moved on to the next gig.
Would that band have gone under the heading of hard bop?

Yeah I would say so because we were playing across things, because you know Benny did a lot of writing of his own. And to this day Benny Golson has never written a weak composition.
